Literature Review

Overview: LoRA [1, 2]
Updates represented as AB^T where A, B are stored low rank matrices
Factorization into (A, B) is non-identifiable as any (AM, BM^{-T}) produces the same update for M invertible
This GL group symmetry is dealt with using GL invariant neural networks or canonicalizing the weights
LoRA weights contain useful information
Can be used for downstream inference tasks
Attribute Classification
Performance prediction
Adapter retrieval

W2T: LoRA Weights Already Know What They Can Do [2]
Handles GL-group symmetry by using SVD as a canonical form and then embedding the weights via a transformer into a ``weight-space''
Embeddings are used for downstream tasks:
Attribute classification: determining attributes of the fine tuning dataset
Performance prediction: predicting performance on benchmark by either ranking or accuracy
Adapter retrieval: pick out LoRA weights that correspond to a specific downstream task from a group of adapters

Limitations/Potential Directions
W2T is a general framework to represent LoRA weights, so it can be adapted to explore further tasks in weight-space learning beyond what the paper has done
Generative modelling: can we learn a distribution over LoRA weights that represents useful knowledge (decoding embedding into usable weights seems to be an unsolved issue)
Other discriminative tasks (classification, regression) or conducting same procedure on different benchmarks (LLM toxicity, alignment)
Ablation studies indicate that the canonicalization of LoRA weights (ie solving the GL-invariant problem) contributes the most to the effectiveness of their method
Rather than using a transformer as the last step to compute embeddings, is it possible to use simpler statistical methods (MDS) to attain comparable results and produce more understandable embeddings
Paper focuses on the simplest case: single LoRA update for fixed model
Can we get reasonable performance on more complicated scenarios such as LoRAs for multiple models, merged LoRAs using their embedding approach
Exploratory: how does merging LoRAs affect their representation in the embedded space? It could be useful to find an embedding such that merging LoRAs represents a simple weighted average procedure, yet still retains effectiveness as inputs to downstream tasks

Efficient Benchmarking Is Just Feature Selection and
Multiple Regression [3]
Addresses the issue of efficient benchmarking: subselect the most distinguishing examples in the benchmark to determine model performance and predict full benchmark scores
Feature Selection
Given M source models, represents each question X_i as a vector in R^M where each component is the score of the model on the particular question and the target Y as the vector of the overall model score on the entire dataset
Then, subselect problems using mRMR (Minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance) based on the problem of predicting Y from X_1, ..., X_N 
Prediction
Uses ridge regression and kernel ridge regression to predict the model score from question scores
Compares to other techniques in accuracy and speed:
Lasso, Anchor Points, IRT

Limitations/Potential Directions
Gives a general framework of decomposing the problem into feature selection and then regression
There are many combinations of different approaches to both problems in the statistics world that have not been explored in the paper
Bayesian Regression/Gaussian Process Regression can be designed to combine both feature selection and regression and resulting distributional information can be extremely informative in understanding the benchmark
Each question has a feature vector that only depends on the performance of fixed source models on it
Could incorporate more information into the feature vector (matrix) to inform decisions, ex:
Concatenate embedding of question text and explore if it makes any meaningful impact on question selection
Representations of ICL and varying prompts
mRMR does not perform as well on continuous valued datasets 
Paper only focuses on in-distribution prediction
Are there any methods following this simple framework that can be competitive in an out of distribution scenario?

Other Interesting Avenues
Comparison of LoRA and DKPS representations
IRT methods
Adaptive benchmarking methods
Select examples depending on model and potential for early stopping
notes:
For adaptive bench and binary, bench fully on several models, construct a graph of the questions where A points to B if getting A right means B is right with high probability (delta_e). Find the smallest number of queries needed to know performance within a selected probability (epsilon) or depending on results of queries, figure out which question to ask next 

Seems like a causal inference problem, but even if the math is done for it, doesn't seem like it has been applied to the benchmarking world
Constructing the graph and looking at clustering on it can give a lot of insight into the types of questions the benchmark covers

Many possible ``levels'' to this:
Unweighted directed graphs: get it by thresholding conditional probabilities, figure out which nodes to sample assuming all probabilities are 1 (just find one node that accesses all other nodes in a component), test on benchmarks (math simple, code simple)
No point in synthetic data since no randomness once graph is known
Unweighted directed graph: get it by thresholding conditional probabilities at epsilon, figure out which nodes to sample assuming all probabilities are at least epsilon to get it within delta accuracy, test on benchmarks (math medium, code medium)
Generate synthetic data using causal inference
Weighted directed graph: get it by setting it as conditional probabilities per edge, figure out which nodes to sample with those probabilities to get it within delta, test on benchmarks (math hard, code hard)
Generate synthetic data using causal inference

Similar things could be done using conditional distributions per edge but would be much harder, perhaps report a predicted range with 95% confidence 
Is there some large sample conditional probability -> true probability/large sample conditional distribution -> true distribution to get asymptotic statistical convergence

Why not just estimate a joint distribution over all items
